messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh is a 52-year-old fast food worker, married with two adult children. For three years she has been unable to shake the night of the flood. The storm had been predicted, but she had believed—naively, she now thinks—that levees would hold. When the water poured through her ground floor apartment at 3 a.m., she grabbed her husband’s arm and they climbed onto the roof. The current was so strong that she lost her grip twice, swallowing dirty water while her husband hauled her back up. They waited on the roof until dawn, listening to the roar and the screams of neighbors. That night rewired something in her. Now, any unexpected loud sound—a dropped tray at the burger chain where she works, a car backfiring in the parking lot—makes her flinch so hard that customers notice. Her manager has asked her twice to “calm down.”

She has come to believe that she will never feel normal emotions again. This conviction sits underneath everything. After the flood, she stopped crying. She stopped laughing. She goes through the motions at work and at home, but inside she is hollow. She also believes she no longer belongs anywhere: her old apartment is gone, her neighborhood rebuilt by strangers, and even her family feels distant. Most deeply, she is certain that she cannot stop bad things from happening. She used to be the one who planned for emergencies, but the flood proved that planning is useless. That sense of helplessness now colors every moment. When she hears a sudden bang at work—the fryer hood slamming shut—her heart seizes because she has already failed to prevent whatever disaster is coming.

Because she believes she is permanently broken and powerless, she has started to dread nightfall. Darkness means the world is unguarded. She lies awake for hours, listening to the creak of the house, the hum of the refrigerator, the distant siren. Sleep is a battle she usually loses. And because she is already on high alert at night, the smallest trigger—a car door closing outside—can send the memory of the flood crashing back: the feel of the water’s pull, the disconnected piece of the neighbor’s cry, the overwhelming rush of fear that makes her sit up in bed, gasping, her whole body shaking. The memory comes in fragments that do not fit together, and when it overwhelms her she has to stop whatever she is doing—counting change, wiping a table—and find a place to stand still until the wave passes.

The cycle tightens at work. Linh’s station is near the drive-through speaker, which crackles and pops unpredictably. Each unexpected sound makes her jump, and each jump brings the flood closer. She has started volunteering for the closing shift, when the restaurant is quieter and the constant clatter is reduced. But even then, the night silence feels dangerous. She cannot relax at home either. Her husband has tried to reassure her, but she feels disconnected from him. She has stopped going to the grocery store after dark, and she dreads the weekends because she cannot avoid the sounds of her own house. What finally brought her to seek help was her daughter’s worried voicemail: “Mom, you don’t talk anymore. You’re like a ghost.” Linh made an appointment at a community clinic. She is terrified that talking will make the memories stronger, but she is also afraid of the alternative—staying trapped at night, forever bracing for the next sound.
